name: Omaha Tribe of Nebraska
land_summary: The Omaha people, the Umóⁿhoⁿ, trace their path west from the Ohio River valley, and by the mid-1700s they lived in earth-lodge villages along the Missouri River in what is now northeast Nebraska. In a treaty signed in Washington on March 16, 1854, the Omaha ceded their lands west of the Missouri south of a set line and kept the land north of it as their home. In 1865 they sold the northern part of that reservation to the United States so the Winnebago could be settled there. Congress opened land on the western side for sale in 1872 and again in 1882; under the 1882 Act about 50,000 acres west of the railroad were sold to settlers, and the town of Pender grew there. The same law provided allotments to Omaha families. In 2016 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the 1882 Act did not shrink the reservation, so Pender lies within it. The tribal government is at Macy, Nebraska.

timeline.event: By the treaty of March 16, signed in Washington, the Omaha cede their lands west of the Missouri south of a set line and keep the northern land as their reservation.
By the treaty of March 6, the Omaha sell the northern part of their reservation to the United States so the Winnebago can be settled there.
Congress authorizes selling land on the western end of the reservation for the tribe's benefit; few parcels sell.
The Act of August 7 opens about 50,000 acres west of the railroad right-of-way to settlers, and the town of Pender is founded there.
In Nebraska v. Parker, decided March 22, the U.S. Supreme Court rules unanimously that the 1882 Act did not diminish the Omaha Reservation.

notes: omaha-nsn.gov refuses automated access. omahatribe.com allows it and identifies itself as the Omaha Tribe of Nebraska, with its office in Macy. Its constitution's Article I (Territory) covers the territory within the present confines of the Omaha Reservation and is used as the boundary statement. The site has no history or homelands narrative (the THPO page is mostly placeholder text), so homelands is null. 'Umóⁿhoⁿ' follows the tribe's own spelling on its site. The 'Ohio River valley' and 'mid-1700s' claims rest on Nebraska Studies and NPS. Left out as single-sourced (Parker opinion only): the 300,000-acre size of the 1854 reservation (Kappler cites 300,000 acres only as a cap on any substitute site), the roughly 98,000 acres sold in 1865, and 50,157 acres as the exact 1882 figure. Current reservation acreage was not found in any nation source and is omitted. 'Disputed' is false because the 2016 ruling settled the western boundary. Change it if reviewers want the history of litigation flagged. The Blackbird Bend lands in Iowa and the related 1970s Supreme Court litigation were not researched.
